extracted.intended_audience: Class VI permit applicants, state and tribal UIC program staff, regulators, and interested stakeholders (industry and public commenters)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements for permitting carbon dioxide geologic sequestration wells (UIC Class VI), including permit components, review criteria, monitoring and reporting, induced seismicity management, environmental justice/public participation, and state primacy processes. Intended to inform applicants, permitting authorities, and reviewers on what is required and how applications are evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major components required in UIC Class VI permits
rubrics_metrics.description: Major components included in UIC Class VI permits are site characterization, area of review, corrective action, well construction and operation, testing and monitoring, financial responsibility, post-injection site care, well plugging, emergency and remedial response, and site closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These components (identified in 40 CFR parts 144-147) form the backbone of a Class VI permit and applicants must provide the requisite information to demonstrate protection of USDWs. Permit writers and applicants should ensure each component is addressed comprehensively in applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect USDWs / prevent migration out of authorized injection zone
rubrics_metrics.description: UIC regulations authorize injection of CO2 for geologic sequestration while protecting human health by ensuring the protection of underground sources of drinking water (USDW); regulations ensure injected CO2 does not migrate out of the authorized injection zone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit review determines whether the application supports a determination that USDWs will not be endangered. Monitoring, testing, proper construction/operation, and post-injection care are all evaluated with this protective objective in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit application review criteria (completeness, technical accuracy, risk-based determination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Review of a UIC permit application entails a multidisciplinary evaluation to determine whether the application includes the required information, is technically accurate, and supports a determination that USDWs will not be endangered by the proposed injection activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA Regions use multidisciplinary experts (geologists, engineers, physical scientists) to assess completeness and technical adequacy. Applicants should submit complete applications and respond promptly to Requests for Additional Information (RAIs) or Notices of Deficiency (NODs) to avoid delays; EPA aims to review complete applications within approximately 24 months but timeframes depend on project complexity and application quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class VI Rule additional protective requirements tailored for geologic sequestration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Class VI Rule includes requirements tailored to large-scale geologic sequestration such as more extensive geologic testing, detailed computational modeling, periodic re-evaluations, detailed monitoring and tracking of the CO2 plume and pressure in the injection zone, unique financial responsibility requirements, and extended post-injection monitoring and site care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These additional requirements address issues unique to CO2 sequestration (large volumes, reservoir pressure, CO2 buoyancy, impurities, corrosivity, mobility). Applicants must provide the technical analyses and plans required by the rule; permitting authorities may impose project-specific measures as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and management of potential migration pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: UIC regulations address major pathways by which injected fluids can migrate into USDWs, including along the injection well bore, via improperly completed or plugged wells in the area near the injection well, direct injection into a USDW, faults or fractures in the confining strata, or lateral displacement into hydraulically connected USDWs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Area of Review (AoR) delineation, site characterization, corrective action plans, and monitoring must specifically consider these pathways. Applicants should evaluate and remediate existing wells and geological features that could provide a migration pathway.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced seismicity identification, monitoring, and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The UIC Class VI program establishes mechanisms to identify, monitor, and reduce risks associated with induced seismicity through permit and program requirements such as site characterization and monitoring, and requires applicants to demonstrate that induced seismic activity will not endanger USDWs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Site-specific seismic strategies may include seismic monitoring (including microseismic), ensuring the confining zone is free of faults of concern, operating limits (e.g., injection pressure below fracture pressure), and contingency responses (stopping or reducing injection). EPA may require seismic monitoring as a permit condition or deny permits if seismic risk could endanger USDWs. Mitigation options include supplemental seismic monitoring, altering rates/pressures, permit modification, partial plug back, controlled restart, suspending/revoking injection authorization, or shutting in the well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seismic data-driven permit conditions and analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: During site characterization, if geologic or seismic data indicate a substantial likelihood of seismic activity, EPA may require further analyses, planned operational changes, and additional monitoring; sufficient pressure buildup, presence of faults of concern, and pathways for pressure communication contribute to induced seismicity risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should include seismic hazard assessments and consider site-specific monitoring and operational controls. Regions are expected to classify and evaluate faults of concern and fracture pressures as part of their review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency and Remedial Response Plan / actions upon leakage
rubrics_metrics.description: If monitoring indicates leakage of injected CO2 from the injection zone, the leakage may trigger a response per the permittee's Class VI Emergency and Remedial Response Plan including halting injection; the permitting authority may prescribe additional permit requirements necessary to prevent movement or take enforcement action if the permit has been violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants must prepare an Emergency and Remedial Response Plan as part of permit requirements. Plans should specify monitoring triggers, response actions (including halting injection), reporting, corrective actions, and communication with the permitting authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: GHGRP subpart RR reporting and MRV requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: GHGRP subpart RR applies to wells injecting CO2 for long-term containment and requires reporting basic information on the mass of CO2 received for injection; development and implementation of an EPA-approved monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) plan; reporting the mass of CO2 sequestered using a mass balance approach; and reporting annual monitoring activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting complements UIC monitoring/testing requirements (see 40 CFR 146.90-91). Facilities with a Class VI permit are generally subject to subpart RR. Reported (non-confidential) data are made publicly available around October each year.

rubrics_metrics.name: MRV plan required components (five major components)
rubrics_metrics.description: An MRV plan must include five major components: (1) delineation of monitoring areas based on the CO2 plume location; (2) identification and evaluation of potential surface leakage pathways and assessment of likelihood, magnitude, and timing of surface leakage; (3) a strategy for detecting and quantifying any surface leakage of CO2 in the event leakage occurs; (4) an approach for establishing expected baselines for monitoring CO2 surface leakage; and (5) a summary of considerations made to calculate site-specific variables for the mass balance equation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MRV plans must be EPA-approved and are intended to quantify CO2 storage and identify/quantify/address potential leakage. Applicants should base MRV design on site geology and the expected plume evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: GHGRP subpart VV (EOR with ISO 27916) and EOR Operations Management Plan (EOR OMP)
rubrics_metrics.description: GHGRP subpart VV applies to geologic sequestration of CO2 associated with EOR operations using ISO 27916 and requires that facilities include in their annual GHGRP report a copy of their EOR Operations Management Plan (EOR OMP). The EOR OMP should describe the EOR complex/engineered system, establish adequacy for safe long-term containment of CO2, and include site-specific information such as geologic characterization, descriptions of facilities and wells, and operations history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilities that choose to submit and report under subpart RR must not also report under subpart VV. Subpart VV is modeled after ISO standard CSA/ANSI ISO 27916:2019. Applicants engaged in EOR should prepare an EOR OMP addressing these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to quantify and publicly report leakage/emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any leakage of CO2 at a sequestration facility must be quantified and reported under GHGRP subpart RR or subpart VV, and such data are made publicly available on the EPA's website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Between 2016-2022, reported leakage/emissions represented <0.5% of reported sequestration; however, surface equipment leaks and venting are common emission sources. Monitoring and reporting systems should capture both subsurface and surface emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class II (EOR) regulation and transition to Class VI when risk increases (40 CFR 144.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: Class II EOR wells are regulated to protect USDWs; however, if the business model for EOR shifts to maximize CO2 injection volumes and permanent storage, the risk to USDWs may increase. The regulations require a Class II operator to obtain a Class VI permit when there is an increased risk to USDWs, based on factors in 40 CFR 144.19(b) such as increase in reservoir pressure, increase in CO2 injection rates, and suitability of the Class II AoR delineation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting authorities may also make the assessment; failure to notify permitting authority when transition is warranted can lead to SDWA enforcement, including cessation of injection. Operators should monitor operational parameters and consult permitting authorities when significant changes occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring, inspections, enforcement, and compliance processes
rubrics_metrics.description: The UIC program works with injection well operators throughout the life of the well to confirm practices do not pose a risk to USDWs, including conducting inspections, evaluating periodic monitoring reports, identifying corrective actions, assisting operators to return to compliance, or using administrative or judicial enforcement to return a well to compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspections verify compliance but are only one compliance tool. Programs should evaluate monitoring reports, issue NODs/RAIs as needed, and require corrective measures. Applicants should design monitoring plans and reporting systems to facilitate regulatory oversight and minimize enforcement risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental justice (EJ) and public participation in Class VI permitting
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA recommends meaningful engagement with local communities and has guidance (Environmental Justice Guidance for UIC Class VI Permitting and Primacy) recommending five themes: (1) identify communities with potential EJ concerns, (2) enhance public involvement, (3) conduct appropriately scoped EJ assessments, (4) enhance transparency throughout the permitting process, and (5) minimize adverse effects to USDWs and the communities they may serve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and EPA Regions should complete an EJ review using the EPA's EJScreen Tool over the applicant's Area of Review (AoR). If potential EJ impacts are identified, consider mitigation measures and enhance outreach (e.g., early targeted outreach, address language barriers and technology/resource limitations) to ensure inclusive participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: State primacy for Class VI and primacy application phases
rubrics_metrics.description: States (and tribes) may apply to the EPA for primacy to administer Class VI programs. The primacy application process has four phases: (1) pre-application activities, (2) completeness review and determination, (3) application evaluation, and (4) rulemaking and codification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Primacy allows states to have primary enforcement authority; applicants and EPA may expect changes to where and how permits are processed as states obtain primacy. EPA provides grants and resources to support primacy development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitting process timing and agency targets
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA aims to review complete Class VI applications and issue permits when appropriate within approximately 24 months, though this timeframe depends on project complexity and application completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA has issued internal guidelines to classify applications (e.g., as major new wells), develop project decision schedules, and set target timeframes for public comment periods, responses to comments, and final decisions. Applicants should submit complete applications and timely responses to avoid prolonging reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proven CO2 retention/trapping mechanisms in justification of sequestration security
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory oversight is built upon understanding proven mechanisms by which CO2 is retained in geologic formations, including structural/stratigraphic trapping, residual trapping, solubility trapping, mineral trapping, and preferential adsorption trapping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should characterize site geology and demonstrate how these mechanisms will contribute to long-term security of injected CO2, and use this understanding to inform modeling, monitoring, and long-term care plans.
